title: Tell prisms from pyramids by their bases and apex

lesson.title: Prisms and Pyramids: Look at the Base!

steps.say: You already know how to sort flat shapes like squares and rectangles by their sides and corners. Today we take one small step up into 3D: how to tell a prism from a pyramid just by looking at the ends.

visual.caption: A 3D solid — let us learn how to name it

steps.say: Here is the whole secret. A prism has two matching flat faces, one at each end. They are the same size and the same shape, like two slices of bread with the filling in between. Those two twin faces are called the bases. A pyramid is different: it has only one base, and all the other faces lean in and meet at a single sharp point on top. That point is called the apex, like the tip of a party hat or a tent pole.

visual.caption: Prism: two matching bases at the ends, no apex

steps.say: Let us try one. Imagine a juice box from your lunch kit, eight centimetres long, five centimetres wide and four centimetres tall. Check the ends: the front face and the back face are both five by four rectangles, exactly matching. Two twin bases, and nowhere does it come to a point. So it is a prism, and because the bases are rectangles we call it a rectangular prism. If all twelve edges were the same, say a six centimetre sugar cube, it would be a cube, which is just a special rectangular prism with square bases.

visual.caption: A cube: every base is a matching square

steps.say: Now the mistake lots of kids make. Suppose the two matching end faces are triangles, and the three faces in between are rectangles. Some kids peek at one of those side rectangles and shout, that is a rectangular prism! But we never name a solid by a side face. We name it by its bases. The twins on the ends are triangles, so it is a triangular prism, not a rectangular one. Always ask first: which two faces match at the ends? That pair is the base, and that pair gives the name.

visual.caption: Side faces are rectangles too — but the bases decide the name

steps.say: So here is your checklist. Two matching bases and no point, it is a prism. One base and everything meeting at one apex, it is a pyramid. Then look at the shape of the base to finish the name.

visual.caption: Two bases, no apex — a prism every time

lesson.answer: Two matching bases and no point means prism; one base rising to a single apex means pyramid — and the base always gives the name.

practice.question: Ms. Yuanyuan has a cereal box from her kitchen. It is thirty centimetres tall, twenty centimetres wide and eight centimetres deep. Every face is a rectangle, the top and the bottom are matching twenty by eight rectangles, and the box does not come to a point anywhere. Draw it yourself if that helps. Is it a prism or a pyramid, and what is its full name? Then say what you would call a solid whose base is a twenty by eight rectangle but whose four side faces all lean in and meet at one sharp point on top.
practice.answer: The cereal box is a prism, because it has two matching bases (the twenty by eight rectangles on top and bottom) and no apex. Its full name is a rectangular prism. The second solid has only one base and all its side faces meet at a single apex, so it is a rectangular pyramid.
